title: Andrea Thamm Publishes New Research on Black Holes and the Nature of Dark Matter : College of Natural Sciences : UMass Amherst
excerpt: If confirmed, Thamm's research could bring scientists closer to observing Hawking radiation and other exciting phenomena.
content:
Content

A mysterious neutrino detected in 2023 could offer new clues about the origins of black holes and the nature of dark matter, according to research highlighted by ZME Science.

Andrea Thamm, a professor in the College of Natural Sciences's Department of Physics, and her colleagues propose that the particle may have originated from the explosive final moments of a primordial black hole—a theoretical object formed in the early universe. Their model suggests that these black holes could possess a mysterious property called "dark charge," potentially explaining why the neutrino was detected by one observatory but not another.

“‘The lighter a black hole is, the hotter it should be and the more particles it will emit,’ explains Andrea Thamm, a physicist at UMass Amherst and co-author of the recent study. ‘As [primordial black holes] evaporate, they become ever lighter, and so hotter, emitting even more radiation in a runaway process until explosion.’”

— ZME Science

If confirmed, Thamm's research could bring scientists closer to observing Hawking radiation, identifying previously unknown particles, and solving one of physics' biggest mysteries: the nature of dark matter.
